source_text: Τὸ μὲν γὰρ, οἷον ἐκ πληγῆς τινος, τῆς προσβολῆς τοῦ ἀβουλήτου τὴν ψυχὴν τύπτοντος καὶ συστέλλοντος, καταθλιβομένου τοῦ περικαρδίου πνεύματος, ἀποτίκτεσθαι πέφυκεν· ἡ δὲ χαρὰ οἷον σκίρτημάτί ἐστι τῆς ψυχῆς ἐπαγαλλομένης τοῖς κατὰ γνώμην. Ὅθεν καὶ τὰ περὶ τὸ σῶμα συμπτώματα διενήνοχε. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ λυπουμένοις ὕπωχρος καὶ πελιδνὸς καὶ κατεψυγμένος ὁ ὄγκος· τοῖς δὲ φαιδρυνομένοις ἐξανθοῦσα καὶ ὑπέρυθρος ἡ τοῦ σώματος ἕξις, μονονουχὶ πηδώσης τῆς ψυχῆς, καὶ προωθουμένης ὑφ' ἡδονῆς εἰς τὸ ἔξω. Πρὸς δὴ ταῦτα ἐροῦμεν, ὅτι καὶ οἱ θρῆνοι καὶ τὰ δάκρυα τῶν ἁγίων διὰ τὴν πρὸς Θεὸν ἀγάπην ἐγίγνοντο. Ἀεὶ οὖν ἐνορῶντες τῷ ἀγαπητῷ, καὶ τὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἑαυτοῖς εὐφροσύνην συναύξοντες, τὰ περὶ τοὺς ὁμοδούλους ἑαυτῶν ᾠκονόμουν· πενθοῦντες τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας, ἐπανορθούμενοι αὐτοὺς διὰ τῶν δακρύων. Ὥσπερ δὲ οἱ ἐπὶ τῶν αἰγιαλῶν ἑστῶτες, τοῖς ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ βαπτιζομένοις συμπάσχοντες, οὐ προΐενται τὴν οἰκείαν ἀσφάλειαν ἐν τῇ περὶ τῶν κινδυνευόντων φροντίδι· οὕτως οὐδὲ οἱ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι τῶν πέλας ἐπιστυγνάζοντες τὴν οἰκείαν ἀφανίζουσιν εὐφροσύνην. Τὸ ἐναντίον μὲν οὖν, καὶ μείζονα ποιοῦσιν αὐτὴν, ὑπὲρ τῶν εἰς τὸν ἀδελφὸν δακρύων τῆς χαρᾶς τοῦ Κυρίου καταξιούμενοι. Διὰ τοῦτο μακάριοι οἱ κλαίοντες, καὶ μακάριοι οἱ πενθοῦντες, ὅτι αὐτοὶ παρακληθήσονται, καὶ αὐτοὶ γελάσουσι. Γέλωτα δὲ λέγει οὐ τὸν διὰ τῶν παρειῶν ἐκπίπτοντα ψόφον ἐν τῷ αἵματος ἀναβρασμῷ, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἄκρατον καὶ ἀμιγῆ παντὸς σκυθρωποῦ ἱλαρότητα. Κλαίειν οὖν μετὰ κλαιόντων συγχωρεῖ ὁ Ἀπό στολος, ἐπειδὴ τὸ δάκρυον τοῦτο οἱονεὶ σπέρμα καὶ δάνεισμα γίνεται τῆς αἰωνίου χαρᾶς. Ἀνάβα μοι τῇ διανοίᾳ, καὶ θέασαι τὴν ἀγγελικὴν κατάστασιν, εἰ ἄλλη τις αὐτοῖς πρέπει κατάστασις, πλὴν τοῦ χαί ρειν καὶ διευθυμεῖσθαι· ὅτι ἠξίωνται παρεστάναι Θεῷ, καὶ ἀπολαύειν τοῦ ἀποῤῥήτου κάλλους τῆς δόξης τοῦ κτίσαντος ἡμᾶς. Πρὸς ἐκεῖνον οὖν τὸν βίον παρορμῶν ἡμᾶς ὁ Ἀπόστολος, πάντοτε χαίρειν ἡμῖν διετάξατο. Ἀλλὰ μὴν πρός γε τὸ δακρῦσαι τὸν Κύριον ἐπὶ Λαζάρῳ καὶ ἐπὶ τῇ πόλει ἐκεῖνο εἰπεῖν ἔχομεν, ὅτι καὶ ἔφαγε, καὶ ἔπιεν, οὐκ αὐτὸς τούτων δεόμενος, ἀλλά σοι μέτρα καὶ ὅρους τῶν ἀναγκαίων τῆς ψυχῆς παθημάτων καταλιμπάνων. Οὕτω γοῦν καὶ ἐδάκρυσε, τῶν ὀδυρτικῶν καὶ φιλοθρήνων τὸ ἄγαν περιπαθὲς καὶ ταπεινὸν ἐπανορθούμενος. Εἰ γάρ τι ἄλλο, καὶ τὸ δακρύειν τῆς ἐκ τοῦ λόγου συμμετρίας προσδεῖται· ἐπὶ τίσι γίνεσθαι, καὶ ἐπὶ πόσον, καὶ πότε, καὶ ὅπως προσῆκεν. Ὅτι γὰρ οὐκ ἐμπαθὲς ἦν τὸ δάκρυον τοῦ Κυρίου, ἀλλὰ διδασκαλικὸν, ἐκεῖθεν δῆλον· Λάζαρος ὁ φίλος ἡμῶν κεκοίμηται, ἀλλὰ πορεύομαι ἵνα ἐξυπνίσω αὐτόν. Τίς ἡμῶν κοιμώμενον ὀδύρεται φίλον, ὃν μικρὸν ὕστερον προσδοκᾷ διυπνίζειν; Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω. Καὶ ὁ νεκρὸς ἐζωοποιεῖτο· καὶ ὁ δεδεμένος περιεπάτει. Θαῦμα ἐν θαύματι· κει ρίαις δεδέσθαι τοὺς πόδας, καὶ μὴ κωλύεσθαι πρὸς τὴν κίνησιν. Μεῖζον γὰρ ἦν τὸ ἐνισχύον τοῦ ἐμ ποδίζοντος. Πῶς οὖν ὁ τοιαῦτα ἐνεργεῖν μέλλων δα κρύων ἄξιον τὸ συμβὰν ἔκρινεν; Ἢ δῆλον, ὅτι, πανταχόθεν τὸ ἀσθενὲς ἡμῶν ὑπερείδων, μέτροις τισὶ καὶ ὅροις τὰ ἀναγκαῖα περιέλαβε πάθη; τὸ μὲν ἀσυμπαθὲς ὡς θηριῶδες ἐκκλίνων, τὸ δὲ φιλόλυπον καὶ πολύθρηνον ὡς ἀγενὲς παραιτούμενος.
thought_title: Tears and joy reconciled; Christ's tears as teaching
orientation: Basil is answering the objection that tears and joy cannot coexist, explaining first their different bodily signs and then how the saints' tears and Christ's tears were measured and instructive.
pass_a_gloss: For the one, as from some blow, when the assault of the unwanted strikes and contracts the soul, when the pericardial breath is compressed, is by nature born; but joy is like a leaping of the soul exulting in things according to its will. Whence also the symptoms concerning the body differ. For in those grieving the bulk is pale and livid and chilled; but in those brightening the condition of the body is blooming and reddish, the soul all but leaping and being pushed forward by pleasure to the outside. To these things then we shall say, that both the laments and the tears of the saints came about through love toward God. Always therefore gazing at the beloved, and increasing for themselves the gladness from there, they managed the things concerning their fellow-servants; mourning those who sin, correcting them through tears. And just as those standing on the shores, suffering together with those being drowned in the sea, do not let go their own safety in the care about those in danger; so neither do those frowning at the sins of neighbors destroy their own gladness. The opposite then, they even make it greater, being deemed worthy of the joy of the Lord on behalf of tears for the brother. Therefore blessed are those who weep, and blessed are those who mourn, because they themselves will be comforted, and they themselves will laugh. But he calls laughter not the noise falling out through the cheeks in the boiling up of blood, but the unmixed and unmingled with anything gloomy cheerfulness. To weep therefore with those weeping the Apostle permits, since this tear becomes as it were a seed and a loan of eternal joy. Go up for me in thought, and behold the angelic state, whether any other state befits them, except to rejoice and be glad; because they have been deemed worthy to stand beside God, and to enjoy the ineffable beauty of the glory of the one who created us. To that life therefore urging us the Apostle commanded us always to rejoice. But indeed, concerning the Lord's weeping over Lazarus and over the city, that we have to say, that he also ate, and drank, not himself needing these things, but leaving to you measures and limits of the necessary sufferings of the soul. Thus indeed he also wept, correcting the excessive passionate and lowly element of those given to wailing and fond of laments. For if anything else, also weeping needs the symmetry that comes from reason: on what occasions it should occur, and how much, and when, and how it is fitting. For that the tear of the Lord was not passionate but instructive, is clear from there: Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep, but I go that I may wake him. Who of us laments a sleeping friend, whom he expects to wake up a little later? Lazarus, come out. And the dead man was made alive; and the bound man walked around. Wonder within wonder: the feet to be bound with grave-cloths, and not to be hindered toward movement. For the strengthening power was greater than the hindering one. How then did the one about to work such things judge the occurrence worthy of tears? Or is it clear, that, supporting our weakness from every side, he enclosed the necessary sufferings with certain measures and limits? Avoiding the unsympathetic as beastly, but rejecting the love of grief and much lamenting as ignoble.

choices.english: when the assault of the unwanted strikes and contracts the soul
choices.why: Keeps the genitive absolute as a temporal clause and preserves the two participles' active force on the soul.
rejected: when the soul is struck and contracted by the assault of the unwanted

choices.english: as it were a seed and a loan
choices.why: Renders the double metaphor literally; δάνεισμα is a loan, not a deposit or pledge.

choices.term: τὴν ἄκρατον καὶ ἀμιγῆ παντὸς σκυθρωποῦ ἱλαρότητα
choices.english: the unmixed and unmingled with anything gloomy cheerfulness
choices.why: Preserves the two adjectives' distinct force and the genitive of separation with ἀμιγῆ.

choices.term: τῶν ὀδυρτικῶν καὶ φιλοθρήνων τὸ ἄγαν περιπαθὲς καὶ ταπεινὸν
choices.english: the excessive passionate and lowly element of those given to wailing and fond of laments
choices.why: Keeps the substantivized adjectives and the genitive of the persons whose trait is corrected.
rejected: the excessive passion and baseness of wailers and lament-lovers

choices.english: the love of grief and much lamenting
choices.why: Renders both substantivized adjectives literally: φιλόλυπον as love of grief, πολύθρηνον as much lamenting.

choices.english: but leaving to you measures and limits
choices.why: Keeps the singular σοι as direct address to the reader, matching Basil's homiletic style.

pass_b_english: Grief is naturally born when the assault of the unwanted strikes and contracts the soul, as if from a blow, while the spirit around the heart is pressed down. Joy, by contrast, is like a leaping of the soul exulting in things that go according to its will. That is why the bodily symptoms also differ. In those who grieve, the body is pale, livid, and chilled; in those who brighten, the body's condition blooms and grows reddish, since the soul all but leaps and is pushed outward by pleasure. To these objections we will say that the laments and tears of the saints came about because of their love for God. Always gazing, then, at the Beloved and increasing the gladness that came to them from there, they managed the affairs of their fellow-servants: mourning those who sinned and correcting them through their tears. Just as people standing on the shore share the suffering of those drowning in the sea but do not surrender their own safety in their concern for those in danger, so also those who grieve over the sins of their neighbors do not destroy their own gladness. On the contrary, they make it greater, since they are counted worthy of the Lord's joy on account of their tears for a brother. For this reason, blessed are those who weep, and blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted, and they will laugh (Matthew 5:4; Luke 6:21). By laughter he does not mean the sound that bursts from the cheeks when the blood boils up, but the cheerfulness that is unmixed and unmingled with anything gloomy. The Apostle therefore permits weeping with those who weep, since this tear becomes, as it were, a seed and a loan of eternal joy. Go up with me in thought and behold the angelic state: what other state befits them except to rejoice and be glad, because they have been counted worthy to stand before God and to enjoy the ineffable beauty of the glory of the One who created us? It is to that life, then, that the Apostle urges us on when he commands us to rejoice always. But as for the Lord's weeping over Lazarus and over the city, we have this to say: he also ate and drank, not because he himself needed these things, but to leave you measures and limits for the necessary sufferings of the soul. So too he wept, correcting the excessive passionate and lowly element of those given to wailing and fond of laments. For if anything needs the symmetry that comes from reason, weeping does: on what occasions it should occur, and to what extent, and when, and how. That the Lord's tears were not passionate but instructive is clear from this: 'Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him' (John 11:11). Who among us mourns a sleeping friend whom he expects to wake a little later? 'Lazarus, come out' (John 11:43). And the dead man was made alive, and the bound man walked. A wonder within a wonder: his feet were bound with grave-cloths, yet he was not hindered from moving. For the power that strengthened him was greater than what impeded him. How then did the One who was about to work such things judge what had happened worthy of tears? Is it not clear that, supporting our weakness from every side, he enclosed the necessary sufferings within measures and limits, avoiding lack of sympathy as beastly, but rejecting the love of grief and much lamenting as ignoble?

problems.quote: Tears are naturally born when the assault of the unwanted strikes and contracts the soul
problems.source_quote: Τὸ μὲν γὰρ, οἷον ἐκ πληγῆς τινος, τῆς προσβολῆς τοῦ ἀβουλήτου τὴν ψυχὴν τύπτοντος καὶ συστέλλοντος, καταθλιβομένου τοῦ περικαρδίου πνεύματος, ἀποτίκτεσθαι πέφυκεν
problems.why: Subject is neuter 'τὸ μὲν' referring to grief/sorrow, not 'tears'; tears introduced later.
problems.fix: Grief is naturally born when the assault of the unwanted strikes and contracts the soul, as if from a blow, while the spirit around the heart is pressed down.

problems.quote: those who frown at the sins of their neighbors
problems.source_quote: οἱ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι τῶν πέλας ἐπιστυγνάζοντες
problems.why: ἐπιστυγνάζοντες means 'grieve over' or 'are downcast at,' not 'frown at' which suggests disapproval rather than sorrow.
problems.fix: those who grieve over the sins of their neighbors
problems.ruling: ἐπιστυγνάζοντες = 'grieving/distressed at' (στυγνάζω); 'frown at' implies disapproval not sorrow, misleading reader.

problems.source_quote: μακάριοι οἱ κλαίοντες, καὶ μακάριοι οἱ πενθοῦντες, ὅτι αὐτοὶ παρακληθήσονται, καὶ αὐτοὶ γελάσουσι
problems.why: Citation is Matthew 5:4, but the quoted text combines Luke 6:21 ('μακάριοι οἱ κλαίοντες νῦν, ὅτι γελάσετε') with Matthew 5:4; Basil conflates both beatitudes.
problems.ruling: Text combines Matt 5:4 and Luke 6:21 (γελάσουσι); citing only Matthew 5:4 misleads reader about source.

fixed: Changed 'Tears' to 'Grief' because the source subject is neuter 'τὸ μὲν' referring to grief/sorrow, not tears.
Changed 'frown at' to 'grieve over' because ἐπιστυγνάζοντες means to be downcast or grieve over, not to frown in disapproval.
Added Luke 6:21 to the citation because Basil conflates Matthew 5:4 with Luke 6:21 in the quoted beatitudes.

sweep.held_why: 1 confirmed problems after 1 repairs; repair made no edit

dismissed.why: Citation reversed: Matthew has 'mourn/comforted' (5:4) and Luke has 'weep/laugh' (6:21), but Basil's combined quote merges both. The English assigns 'weep' to Matthew and 'laugh' to Luke, but Matthew 5:4 says 'mourn' not 'weep', and Luke 6:21 says 'weep' and 'laugh' not 'mourn'. The parenthetical attribution is garbled.
dismissed.note: Basil blends Matthew 5:4 (mourn, comforted) with Luke 6:21 (weep, laugh), and citing both is exactly right.
